acceptedAnswer.text:
Per square metre of area treated rather than per piece. Counting gum is impractical and it also prices the wrong thing: the time goes into treating the shadows, not into lifting the gum.

For a regular arrangement it is priced per visit on an agreed frequency, which works out considerably cheaper than periodic catch-ups.

mainEntity.name: Will the marks come out completely?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Caught within months, usually yes. Gum that has been trodden into porous concrete for years has pressed dirt deep into the surface and the honest outcome is a significant improvement rather than invisibility.

On a footpath being treated for the first time in a decade, the result is a uniformly clean surface with some faint marks rather than a grid of dark circles.

mainEntity.name: Can you do it outside trading hours?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a retail footpath it is the only sensible option, and it is the default. Before opening or after close, so there is no equipment across a doorway while customers are trying to use it.

mainEntity.name: How often does a shopfront footpath need doing?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Quarterly to twice yearly for most retail, and monthly for a very high traffic entry like a shopping centre door or a transport interchange.

Frequency is what keeps the cost down, because fresh gum lifts easily and old gum needs the full shadow treatment.

mainEntity.name: Is the council footpath our responsibility?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Legally it varies by council and it is worth checking. Practically, nobody walking past distinguishes between your tiles and the council's concrete two steps away, so the strip in front of a retail frontage gets read as part of the shop.

Most retailers deal with the footpath directly outside their entrance regardless of who technically owns it.
